sources.title: Indisch Herinneringscentrum, prewar political and military developments
sources.note: Rulers, Ethical Policy and Nationalism sections describe a diverse archipelago, Dutch reliance on Indigenous officials, limited education and administration openings, and the rise and repression of nationalism.

sources.title: Indisch Herinneringscentrum, overview of the prewar Netherlands Indies
sources.note: Museum education overview: by about 1900 the Dutch claimed nearly the whole archipelago, the Ethical Policy promised greater welfare and autonomy, nationalism grew, and colonial modernization remained unequal and contested.

sources.title: The Colonial State: Violence and Modernity, Resistance and Repression
sources.note: Open-access MERDEKA chapter, especially printed pages 20 to 21: coercive state formation and the paternalistic Ethical Policy, whose education, irrigation and migration programs also served colonial labor and production needs.

sources.title: Dis/connection: Violence, Religion, and Geographic Imaginings in Aceh and Colonial Indonesia, 1890s to 1920s
sources.note: Itinerario open-access article, especially web lines 493 to 522: Dutch conquest used brutal violence and territorial categories; victory was claimed in the late 1910s but armed resistance on Aceh’s west coast persisted.

sources.title: From Across the Water: Nusakambangan and the Making of a Notorious Prison Island
sources.note: International Review of Social History, web lines 564 to 579: centralized prisons, forced labor, deported Acehnese, Buginese and Toraja prisoners, colonial legal categories, incomplete statistics and the press-shaped reputation of Nusakambangan.

sources.title: Two Sides of the Same Coin: Direct Taxation and Negotiated Governance in Colonial Indonesia
sources.note: Journal of Social History, Fairness and Equality section, web lines 91 to 104: racialized sociolegal classes connected residents to separate bureaucracies, laws, courts and tax practices that were unevenly negotiated.

sources.title: Activities of the Indonesian Political Parties During the Early Years of the People’s Council, Part I
sources.note: Japan Society for Southeast Asian Studies abstract, web lines 137 to 143: Volksraad founded in May 1918, indirect election through unequal local councils, advisory authority, nationalist disappointment and four Budi Utomo members among ten elected Indigenous members.

sources.title: Indie Weerbaar Polemic and the Radicalization of Sarekat Islam, 1917 to 1918
sources.note: Indonesian Historical Studies abstract, web lines 20 to 42: dispute over an Indies defense force, Abdoel Moeis, Semaoen, decentralized Sarekat Islam branches, labor politics and the Radicale Concentratie in the Volksraad.

sources.title: Translating and Transliterating Marxism in Indonesia
sources.note: Modern Asian Studies, web lines 552 to 569: 1914 ISDV, railway-union ties, Dutch and Malay political print, Sarekat Islam connections, Sinar Hindia in 1918, Soeara Ra’jat in 1919 and the 1920 party renaming.

sources.title: Print Power and Censorship in Colonial Indonesia, 1914 to 1942
sources.note: Cornell dissertation, chapter on press offences: Semaun translated a Sneevliet article into Malay for Sinar Hindia, considered the danger, published it with an editorial on 16 November 1918, and faced colonial prosecution.

sources.title: Spreading Nationalism in the Early 1900s: Marco Kartodikromo’s Radical Newspapers
sources.note: University historical journal article, section on Marco and Sinar Hindia: a 1918 article used the period Malay title “Azia boeat Orang Azia,” translated by the authors as “Asia is for Asian people.”

sources.title: The Netherlands Indies and the Great War, open-access monograph
sources.note: Open-access scholarly monograph, especially the August 1914 and wartime economy chapters: Dutch neutrality, shipping disruption, rice export bans and price controls, colonial commodity bottlenecks and expanding government economic intervention.

sources.title: Commodities and anti-commodities: Rice on Sumatra, 1915 to 1925
sources.note: Wageningen peer-reviewed chapter abstract, web lines 32 to 45: wartime shipping anxiety, Sumatran estates’ dependence on migrant contract labor and imported rice, rising prices, and 1918 restrictions on food-crop exports.

sources.title: The Price of Un/Freedom: Indonesia’s Colonial and Contemporary Plantation Labor Regimes
sources.note: Comparative Studies in Society and History, Tobacco and Rubber section: Sumatran export estates, Chinese and Javanese migrant recruitment, coercive contracts, penal sanctions and worker desertion in the colonial plantation regime.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, family and Purworejo sugar-factory album, RP-F-F01051
sources.note: Public-domain album catalogue: family photographs mainly from 1916 to 1918 plus Purworejo sugar-factory scenes, verandas, cars, swimming, tennis, children, rice pounding, household workers and unnamed Indonesian subjects.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, Indonesian house servant serving a European man at table, April 1917
sources.note: Public-domain photograph RP-F-F01051-8-3, dated April 1917. The catalogue identifies an Indonesian house servant, a European man, dining room and anonymous photographer, but does not name the worker.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Traditional Settlement at Nagari Sijunjung
sources.note: Indonesia’s UNESCO tentative-list nomination: nine Minangkabau clans, female-line descent and inheritance, matrilocal marriage, rumah gadang, maternal male relatives, elected penghulu, customary teaching, mosques, fields and markets. Used as continuity evidence, not a 1914 census.

sources.title: The modernity of tradition: Women and “healthy progress” in late colonial Java and Sumatra
sources.note: Modern Asian Studies, especially web lines 513 to 535 and 559 to 610: 1919 Malay press discussion, women’s agency in negotiating health and child-rearing, consumer advertising, hygiene propaganda, promised wells and latrines, and colonial blame.

sources.title: Education, Labour, and Discipline: Indigenous Children in Colonial Asia
sources.note: International Review of Social History, web lines 533 to 541: slow village-school implementation, local cost burdens, no comprehensive system, no more than five percent of Indigenous children receiving several official school years around 1905, and unequal investment.

sources.title: Kartini and Van Deventer Schools: pioneers of girls’ schooling in colonial Semarang
sources.note: Indonesian education-history article using Kartini Fund records: Semarang school opened in 1913; Madiun, Batavia and Buitenzorg followed in 1914, Malang in 1915, Cirebon and Pekalongan in 1916; first-year Semarang pupils were ages seven to thirteen.

sources.title: Museum Benteng Vredeburg, diorama of Muhammadiyah’s founding
sources.note: Official Indonesian cultural-heritage page: Ahmad Dahlan and colleagues founded Muhammadiyah in Kauman, Yogyakarta, on 18 November 1912 amid concerns about education, social conditions and colonial discrimination.

sources.title: Universitas Indonesia Archive, the STOVIA and Salemba medical-school buildings
sources.note: Official UI archive, web lines 51 to 69: nine-year STOVIA curriculum, compulsory dormitory and facilities, 1916 cornerstone, 1919 central teaching hospital, and the 1920 move to Salemba with a later choice of dormitory or lodging.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum collection, boys on a raft at Kali Taman
sources.note: Rijksmuseum subject catalogue lists the public-domain photograph “Jongens op een vlot bij Kali Taman in Nederlands-Indië,” anonymous, circa 1917. It records a moment of play without identifying the boys.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum collection, men pounding rice with older equipment
sources.note: Rijksmuseum subject catalogue lists an anonymous circa 1916 to 1917 photograph of men pounding rice with older tools in the Netherlands Indies; the catalogue does not name the men or location.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, warung with food displayed on a table in inland Java
sources.note: Public-domain stereograph RP-F-2001-17-184, inland Java or Malang possibly, dated broadly 1900 to 1935. Its catalogue identifies a warung and displayed food but no dish, vendor or customer.

sources.title: Rijksmuseum, a market in Grobogan
sources.note: Rijksmuseum catalogue for anonymous photograph RP-F-2005-162-1, dated 1910 to 1928 and located at a market in Grobogan, Java. Used only for the visible setting and cautious source criticism.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Javanese Headcloth, 58.33.4
sources.note: Met object record, web lines 3 to 49: mid-nineteenth to early twentieth-century Pekalongan cotton headcloth, local wrapping traditions, everyday and formal use, faux-patchwork tambal design and sometimes protective meanings.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Javanese Sarong, 22.167.3
sources.note: Met object record: north-coast Javanese cotton batik, mid-nineteenth to early twentieth century; tubular garment format, body and head design zones, changing status rules, Chinese-community fashion and Indian and Chinese motifs.

sources.title: The Rijksmuseum Bulletin, colonial archaeology and Candi Panataran
sources.note: Rijksmuseum Bulletin article, printed page 266: the Archaeological Service began full restoration at Candi Panataran in 1918; Javanese dignitaries joined an advisory committee and results were shared with students and teachers.

sources.title: The expansion of medical education in the Dutch East Indies and the Indonesian medical profession
sources.note: Medical History, web lines 514 to 522 and 562: STOVIA, Surabaya’s 1913 NIAS, Indigenous physicians’ training, dormitory and laboratory education, social and professional struggles, and arguments that trusted Indonesian doctors understood patients’ concerns.

sources.title: Medical Journal of Indonesia, The History of Pathology in Indonesia
sources.note: University medical-history article: NIAS opened in Surabaya in 1913, the term Indisch Arts replaced Inlandsch Arts in 1913, and a cancer institute was established in Bandung in 1914 among a small set of pathology centers.

sources.title: Species sanitation of malaria in the Netherlands East Indies, 1913 to 1942
sources.note: Medical-history review, web lines 57 to 75 and 79 to 123: 1915 to 1919 Sumatra trials, Surabaya work, Belawan intervention in 1919, identifying local mosquito habitats, engineering measures and incomplete early trials.

sources.title: The 1918 to 1920 Influenza Pandemic: A Retrospective in the Time of COVID-19
sources.note: Cambridge Elements PDF, printed pages 26 to 27: colonial vital statistics heavily favored European and “other foreign” residents, Java data were deficient, estimates are disputed, and a careful reconstruction estimated about 1.47 million excess deaths in Java.

sources.title: Hygiënische toestanden in Nederlandsch Indië, 1917 review of a 1914 water survey
sources.note: Contemporary Dutch review in DBNL, pages 36 to 37: a 1914 survey reported severely inadequate drinking, bathing and washing water, few urban pipes or hydrants, polluted rivers and wells, and one river serving as toilet, urinal and fishery.

sources.title: Establishment of a specialized health administration through plague control in the Dutch East Indies, 1900 to 1925
sources.note: Socio-Economic History abstract, web lines 62 to 66: Java plague from 1911, new Civil Medical Service, diagnostic spleen puncture, isolation and ratproofing, community skepticism, failed uniform measures and a shift toward locally adapted research.

sources.title: Wereldmuseum Amsterdam, Health care in the Netherlands Indies
sources.note: Museum research page, web lines 23 to 154: poverty and unhealthy conditions, cholera and plague, vaccination, home rebuilding, quinine, missions, small urban medical workforce and health services that remained insufficient across the archipelago.

sources.title: Institut Teknologi Bandung, History
sources.note: Official university history: the Bandung technical college opened on 3 July 1920 with one faculty and a road and water engineering major; its first 1920 to 1921 class had 28 students, only two Indonesian.

sources.title: Indisch Herinneringscentrum, the road to Japanese occupation
sources.note: Invasion and Indies government sections: Japan took Tarakan in January 1942, landed on Java on 1 March after the Java Sea defeat, and forced the Dutch colonial government out of the archipelago.

sources.title: Nationaal Archief, Transfer of sovereignty to Indonesia, 1949
sources.note: Dutch National Archives education source: Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945; the Netherlands refused, war followed, and sovereignty was transferred on 27 December 1949, initially excluding western New Guinea.

scopeNotes: New text needs independent review; earlier hashes do not certify it.
Map endpoints are not historical founding or extinction dates.
Agent researched a disjoint batch; integration and structural checks are not independent historical certification.
Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: The 1914 to 1920 Netherlands Indies was a diverse, unequal colonial state shaped by wartime shortages, resistance, expanding schools and print, public-health crises and growing political organization; its 1920 cutoff is only an atlas handoff.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact target netherlands-indies is indexed circa 1914 to 1920 and is missing before integration.
The world-1914 target has 15 parts/rings and 908 positions; it is exactly identical to the 1900 predecessor shape labeled Netherlands Indies under netherlands-1878.
The world-1920 successor dutch-east-indies-1920 preserves the same topology dimensions; its maximum coordinate delta is about 0.00136 degrees because the TopoJSON transform changes.
The 1920 endpoint is a map-library id handoff, not a historical end of the colony.
Coarse geometry misses some known coastal cities in point tests; the card calls it a locator, never a verified sovereignty polygon.
Related dutch-east-indies, netherlands-1878 and dutch-east-indies-1920 cards remain distinct; no appliesTo linkage is used.
